sras-s1.title: Costs and productivity in Country V

table.caption: Country V, year by year: average nominal wage, price of oil and output per worker (invented data for practice)

sras-s2.title: A shift in Country W's short-run aggregate supply

items.q: Based on the table, in which year did Country V's SRAS curve shift to the left compared with Year 1, because of an input price?
options: Year 2
Year 3
Year 1
No year, because the price level is not in the table

why.correct: Higher oil prices raise firms' costs at every price level, so they supply less real output: SRAS shifts left.
options: Right: oil rose from 60 to 90 dollars a barrel with wages and output per worker unchanged, so costs per unit rose.
In Year 3 output per worker rose with costs unchanged, which shifts SRAS right.
Year 1 is the starting point the other years are compared with.
SRAS shifts with input prices and productivity at a given price level. The table shows exactly those.

items.q: Based on the table, what happened to SRAS in Year 3 compared with Year 1?
options: It shifted left, because firms needed fewer workers
It shifted right, as output per worker rose
It did not change, because wages and oil prices were the same
The economy moved up along SRAS to a higher price level

why.correct: Output per worker rose from 10 to 11 with wages and oil unchanged: cost per unit fell, so SRAS shifted right.
options: Producing more per worker lowers cost per unit; that raises supply, it does not lower it.
Right: higher productivity lowers the cost of each unit, so firms supply more at every price level.
Input prices did not change, but productivity rose, and productivity also shifts SRAS.
Nothing in the table is the price level; a rise in productivity shifts the curve.

items.q: Using the table, calculate the percent change in Country V's average nominal wage from Year 1 to Year 4.

mistakes.why: 2 is the change in dollars. The percent change divides it by the starting wage: $\frac{2}{20} \times 100$.
You started from Year 4. Percent change is measured from the starting value, Year 1.

items.q: In Year 4 the nominal wage rose while output per worker was the same as in Year 1. What does this do to SRAS, and why?
options: It shifts right, because workers with higher pay spend more
It does not shift, because wages are not an input price
It shifts left, because the labor cost of each unit of output rose
It moves along SRAS to more output

why.correct: Higher nominal wages with no gain in productivity raise firms' costs at every price level, so SRAS shifts left.
options: Workers' spending is part of AD. For firms, wages are a cost, so SRAS shifts left.
Nominal wages are the price of labor, a key input. They shift SRAS.
Right: wages are the largest input cost; higher wages with the same productivity raise cost per unit.
A change in an input price shifts SRAS; only a change in the price level moves along it.

items.q: Which event could have caused the shift shown in the graph, from SRAS1 to SRAS2?
options: A new technology that lets workers produce more each hour
A fall in household wealth that cuts consumption
A government subsidy paid to firms for each unit they produce
A sharp rise in the price of energy used by most firms

why.correct: SRAS2 lies to the left of SRAS1: at each price level firms supply less, as when an input such as energy gets dearer.
options: Higher productivity lowers costs and shifts SRAS right, not left.
A fall in consumption shifts AD left; it does not move SRAS.
A subsidy lowers firms' costs and shifts SRAS right.
Right: higher energy prices raise production costs at every price level, so SRAS shifts left.

items.q: According to the graph, what does the shift mean at a price level that stays the same?
options: Firms supply less real output at that price level than before
Firms supply more real output at that price level than before
Households plan to buy less real output at that price level
Firms charge a lower price level for the same output

why.correct: SRAS2 is to the left of SRAS1, so at any given price level firms now supply less real GDP.
options: Right: a leftward shift means less output supplied at each price level.
That would be a shift to the right. SRAS2 is to the left of SRAS1.
Planned buying is AD, which did not shift in the graph.
A leftward SRAS shift means each output level now needs a higher price level, not a lower one.

items.q: Which of the following could each cause the shift in the graph? Select all that apply.
options: Nominal wages rise across the economy with no gain in productivity
A new tax on each unit firms produce
Firms buy faster machines that raise output per worker
The price level rises

why.correct: Anything that raises firms' costs per unit at a given price level, such as wages or a tax per unit, shifts SRAS left.
options: Right: higher labor costs per unit shift SRAS left.
Right: a tax per unit adds to firms' costs and shifts SRAS left.
Higher productivity lowers costs; SRAS shifts right.
A change in the price level moves along SRAS; it does not shift it.

items.q: Why does the short-run aggregate supply curve slope upward?
options: A higher price level makes households richer, so they buy more
Sticky wages make extra output more profitable when the price level rises
Workers demand higher wages whenever output rises
A higher price level brings more workers into the country, so output rises

why.correct: In the short run, wages set by contract and some sticky prices do not adjust at once, so a higher price level makes more output profitable.
options: That is about spending (AD), and a higher price level lowers real wealth rather than raising it.
Right: output prices rise while many costs stay fixed for a while, so firms produce more.
If wages rose as fast as prices, profits would not rise and firms would not expand. It is wage stickiness that gives the slope.
The slope comes from fixed costs and contracts in the short run, not from migration.

items.q: The price level rises by 5 percent, but workers' wage contracts will not be renegotiated for a year. What happens in the short run?
options: Firms produce less, because the price level is higher
SRAS shifts right, because firms' profits rose
Firms produce more, since prices rose but wage costs did not
Nothing changes until the wage contracts are renegotiated next year

why.correct: Sticky nominal wages mean a higher price level raises profit per unit, so firms move up along SRAS to more output.
options: A higher price level with sticky wages makes extra output more profitable, so output rises.
The price level is on the axis; its change moves along SRAS rather than shifting it.
Right: that is a movement up along SRAS.
Firms respond at once to higher selling prices; only wages wait for the contracts.

items.q: Workers across the economy come to expect prices to rise faster next year, and they bargain for higher nominal wages now. What happens to SRAS?
options: It shifts right, because firms expect to sell at higher prices
It does not move, because nothing has happened to prices yet
The economy moves along SRAS to a higher price level
It shifts left, because firms' wage costs rise at every price level

why.correct: When workers expect faster price growth, they ask for higher nominal wages; that raises costs and shifts SRAS left.
options: Expecting higher prices raises wage demands, which raises costs; that shifts SRAS left.
Wages are bargained on what workers expect, so costs rise now.
A change in wages is a change in costs, which shifts the curve.
Right: what workers expect about prices feeds into wages, and higher wages shift SRAS left.

items.q: A drought ruins harvests and raises the cost of food used by restaurants, food processors and other firms. Shift the right curve to show the effect.

why.correct: Higher input costs shift SRAS to the left; AD does not move.

key.because: a rise in the cost of an input

slips.AD: A drought raises what it costs firms to produce. That shifts SRAS, not spending (AD).

items.q: The government pays firms a subsidy for each unit of output they produce. Shift the right curve to show the effect.

why.correct: A subsidy per unit lowers firms' costs, so SRAS shifts to the right.

key.because: a subsidy that lowers firms' costs

slips.AD: The subsidy goes to firms for producing, so it lowers costs and shifts SRAS, not AD.

items.q: Nothing shifts, but the price level rises. Mark a point X on the SRAS curve showing the new price level and real output supplied.

why.correct: A higher price level is a movement up along SRAS: a higher price level and more real output.

items.q: Which change moves an economy along its SRAS curve instead of shifting it?
options: A rise in the price level
A rise in nominal wages
A rise in productivity
A fall in the price of oil

why.correct: Only the variable on an axis moves the economy along the curve. Input prices, productivity and taxes on firms shift it.
options: Right: the price level is on the vertical axis, so its change is a movement along SRAS.
Wages are an input price; a change in them shifts SRAS.
Productivity changes cost per unit and shifts SRAS.
Oil is an input; a change in its price shifts SRAS.

items.q: Make it specific: explain how a fall in oil prices affects short-run aggregate supply.

why.correct: Cheaper oil lowers production costs, so firms supply more at every price level: SRAS shifts right.

specific.frame: Oil prices fall, so firms' production costs ___. At every price level firms supply ___ real output, so ___ shifts to the ___.
specific.model: Oil prices fall, so firms' production costs decrease. Because each unit is cheaper to make, firms supply more real output at every price level, so SRAS shifts to the right.

change.label: Costs
options: fall
rise

why.1: Oil is an input, so cheaper oil lowers costs.

output.label: Output supplied
options: more
less

why.1: Lower costs make more output profitable at each price level.

curve.label: The curve
options: SRAS
AD

why.1: Costs of production change supply, not planned spending.

direction.label: Which way
options: right
left

why.1: More output supplied at each price level is a shift right.

items.q: A country's government adds many new safety rules that raise firms' costs of producing each unit. What happens to SRAS?
options: It shifts right
It shifts left
It does not change, because rules are not prices
It becomes vertical

why.correct: Government rules and taxes that raise firms' costs shift SRAS left; subsidies shift it right.
options: Higher costs mean less supply at each price level, not more.
Right: rules that raise costs per unit lower the output firms supply at each price level.
Rules that raise costs work like a higher input price: they shift SRAS.
The slope comes from sticky wages and prices in the short run; a cost increase shifts the curve.

items.q: Which of the following would shift SRAS to the right? Select all that apply.
options: A fall in the price of oil used by most firms
A rise in consumer spending
A rise in the price level
A rise in nominal wages across the economy

why.correct: SRAS shifts right when production costs per unit fall at a given price level, as with cheaper oil.
options: Right: cheaper inputs lower costs at every price level.
Spending shifts AD, not SRAS.
The price level is on the axis: its change moves along SRAS.
Higher wages raise costs and shift SRAS left.
